title: Pizza in Teglia
subtitle: Deep-pan pizza in a tin, Roman style
excerpt: Pizza in teglia is a thick, soft-crumbed pizza baked in a well-oiled tin. The olive oil fries the base against the metal while the top browns in the oven heat. It is deeper and more substantial than pizza al taglio and works as a full dinner rather than a snack.

recipe.yieldDescription: 1 deep-pan pizza in a 25 x 35 cm tin, serving 4 as a main
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in slices. Reheat at 200°C for 12 to 15 minutes straight from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough proves at room temperature for 2 hours. For a lighter crumb, make it the night before and prove in the fridge overnight.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan or conventional. Preheat the tin in the oven for 10 minutes before adding the dough.

content.text: Pizza in teglia is a thick, tin-baked pizza with a soft, open crumb and a base that fries slightly in the olive oil coating the tin. It is deeper and more filling than a Neapolitan pizza and is designed to be a full meal for four people. The dough is soft and a little sticky, which makes it much easier to handle than a lean pizza dough.

items.prepNote: 3 for the tin, 2 for the dough

content.text: Combine the flour, yeast, salt, water, and 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large bowl. Mix until a soft, sticky dough forms. Knead for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and leave at room temperature for 1.5 to 2 hours until doubled in size.
Pour 3 tablespoons of olive oil into the tin and spread it around. Heat the oven to 230°C with the tin inside for 10 minutes.
Tip the proved dough into the hot oiled tin. Press it out with oiled fingers to fill the tin completely. If it springs back, leave it for 10 minutes.
Season the passata with salt and spread it over the dough. Scatter the mozzarella, sprinkle with oregano, and drizzle with a little more olive oil.
Bake for 28 to 32 minutes until deep golden on top and the base lifts away cleanly from the tin. Cool for 10 minutes before cutting into squares.

Pizza in teglia sits between pizza and focaccia: thicker than a Neapolitan pizza, thinner than a Sicilian sfincione. It is the most forgiving version to make at home because the high-sided tin holds the dough in shape and the olive oil creates a crisp, almost fried base without needing a pizza stone. The topping can vary as much as you like once you have the base technique.
